rows.description: A child assumes the tall, cheerful classmate is also smart and honest. One good trait spreads into a general glow.
A teenager believes whatever a talented or good-looking influencer says about health or money, because admiration in one area carries over to everything.
A teenager says that one is not okay in a calm voice, or changes the subject. Naming a boundary once, clearly, is stronger than laughing it off, and good friends adjust.
Someone realises a joke hurt and says I am sorry, that was not okay, without adding but you are too sensitive. A clean apology repairs trust faster than a defence of intent.

rows.subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
rows.description: A tired toddler often looks more hyper than drowsy, running, laughing too loudly, then crashing into tears. Adults who read this as misbehaviour miss the cue that bedtime or a nap is overdue.

rows.subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
rows.description: A teacher sees a normally cheerful child slumped, irritable and slow to start work. Asking gently about bedtime, homework load or noise at home is more useful than a punishment for inattention.
A colleague notices repeated small mistakes, flat humour and shortness in a usually sharp teammate. A private, kind check-in about workload and rest helps more than gossip or criticism of the errors.
A child sees an adult's neutral face and wrongly reads anger or dislike. Adults can say they are just thinking, and children learn a face is not always a mood.

rows.subtype: Tense or rigid face under threat [Interpreting]
rows.description: A teenager notices a friend's rigid, frozen face after upsetting news and understands it may mean shock or fear, not indifference. Quiet support and time are better than demanding a reaction.

rows.subtype: Blank expression in exhaustion or burnout [Interpreting]
rows.description: A colleague with a blank face for weeks may be exhausted, low or overloaded, not uninterested. A private, kind check-in and practical help matter more than judging attitude.
A toddler hands over a toy, hugs, or says a prompted "thank you" after a gift. The gesture often follows adult modelling and may carry real pleasure before it carries a grasp of gratitude.

A teenager shows admiration with likes, comments, hearts or a shared post. Such signals are quick and low-cost, so their sincerity varies; a specific personal message usually means more than a reaction count.
A young professional credits a teammate's contribution in a meeting or message. Specific, timely and public credit builds trust, while generic praise or taking shared credit damages it.
A child notices that the days he wears his red shirt are the days his team wins and decides the shirt causes it. Things that happen together seem linked.
A teenager sees that students who take tuition score higher and concludes tuition is the cause, missing that motivated or better-off students do both.
A student reads that coffee drinkers live longer and starts believing coffee is the reason. Hidden third factors, or reversed direction, often explain links.
